knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Logarithm With a Calculator Using the Change of Base Formula

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's calculate $\log_{13}(10)$ by changing the base $13$ to the common logarithm (base $10$).

We use the change of base formula:

$$
\log_a X=\frac{\log_b X}{\log_b a}
$$

In our case, $a=13,$ $X=10,$ $b=10.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\log_{13}(10) & =\frac{\log_{10}(10)}{\log_{10}(13)} \\ & =\frac{\log(10)}{\log(13)} \\ & \approx \frac{1}{1.113943} \\ & \approx 0.898\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: integer a>1, X>1; a!=10; no common integer-power base for a and X
generation.sampling_policy: Practice requires numerical change of base; replay retains original evidence.

question.:question/problem: Use a calculator to evaluate $\log_{22}(19)$ rounded to $2$ decimal places.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's calculate $\log_{22}(19)$ by changing the base $22$ to the common logarithm (base $10$).

We use the change of base formula:

$$
\log_a X=\frac{\log_b X}{\log_b a}
$$

In our case, $a=22,$ $X=19,$ $b=10.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\log_{22}(19) & =\frac{\log_{10}(19)}{\log_{10}(22)} \\ & =\frac{\log(19)}{\log(22)} \\ & \approx \frac{1.27875}{1.34242} \\ & \approx 0.95\end{aligned}
$$
